q: Thermodynamics is the branch of science that deals with:
o: Energy changes that accompany physical and chemical processes
The rates at which chemical reactions take place
The step-by-step mechanism of chemical reactions
The arrangement of atoms inside crystal lattices
x: Thermodynamics studies energy changes and the interconversion of heat and other forms of energy. Rates and mechanisms belong to chemical kinetics.

q: Which of the following can thermodynamics NOT tell us about a chemical reaction?
o: Whether heat is released or absorbed
The size of the enthalpy change
How heat and work are related to the energy change
x: Thermodynamics deals with initial and final states and energy changes, not time. The speed of a reaction is a question for chemical kinetics.

q: Thermochemistry is best defined as the study of:
o: Changes in reaction rate with temperature
Light emitted by atoms on heating
Heat changes that accompany chemical reactions
x: Thermochemistry is the part of thermodynamics that deals with heat changes in chemical reactions. Electricity from reactions is electrochemistry; rate changes are kinetics.

q: Thermodynamics describes a system mainly in terms of:
o: The motion of one particular molecule in a collision
The path of electrons during bond breaking
The time a reaction takes to reach equilibrium
Bulk properties such as pressure, volume and temperature
x: Thermodynamics works with macroscopic (bulk) properties of matter like P, V and T. It does not follow individual molecules or time.

q: Which of the following is a spontaneous process?
o: Heat flowing by itself from a cold body to a hot body
Water splitting into hydrogen and oxygen by itself
x: A spontaneous process happens on its own without outside help, like water flowing downhill. The other three need energy supplied from outside.

q: Which statement about spontaneous processes is correct?
o: Every spontaneous process is very fast
A spontaneous process needs a continuous supply of outside energy
Some spontaneous processes absorb heat, such as ammonium chloride dissolving in water
x: Dissolving NH₄Cl in water is spontaneous yet absorbs heat, so being exothermic is not a requirement. Spontaneous does not mean fast, and it needs no continuous outside energy.

q: For the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), which question can thermodynamics answer?
o: How long the mixture takes to reach equilibrium
Which catalyst gives the fastest rate
How much heat is evolved per mole of ammonia formed
What the order of the reaction is
x: Heat evolved is an energy change, which thermodynamics deals with. Time, catalyst speed and order of reaction are kinetic questions.

q: Which statement about a non-spontaneous process is correct?
o: It can never be made to happen under any conditions
It always releases heat to the surroundings
It always happens faster than a spontaneous process
It can be made to happen by supplying energy from outside, as in the electrolysis of water
x: A non-spontaneous change such as splitting water can be driven by an external energy source like electricity. It does not occur on its own.

q: For an exothermic reaction:
o: ΔH is positive and heat is given out to the surroundings
ΔH is negative and heat is given out to the surroundings
ΔH is negative and heat is taken in from the surroundings
ΔH is positive and heat is taken in from the surroundings
x: In an exothermic reaction the products have less enthalpy than the reactants, so ΔH is negative and heat passes to the surroundings.

q: Which of the following reactions is endothermic?
o: Thermal decomposition of CaCO₃ into CaO and CO₂
Formation of water from hydrogen and oxygen
x: Heat must be supplied continuously to decompose calcium carbonate, so ΔH is positive. Combustion, neutralisation and formation of water all release heat.

q: Which change is exothermic?
o: Freezing of liquid water to ice
x: Freezing releases heat as the particles settle into a solid. Melting, evaporation and sublimation all need heat to be absorbed.

q: Solid ammonium nitrate is dissolved in water and the beaker feels cold. This shows that the dissolving process:
x: The process takes heat from the water, so the solution cools. Heat absorbed means the process is endothermic and ΔH is positive.

q: For N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g), ΔH = +180 kJ. Which statement is correct?
o: 180 kJ of heat is released to the surroundings
The reactants have a higher enthalpy than the products
The products have a higher enthalpy than the reactants
90 kJ of heat is released for each mole of NO formed
x: A positive ΔH means heat is absorbed, so the enthalpy of 2NO is 180 kJ above that of N₂ and O₂. No heat is released.

q: A reaction is exothermic when:
o: The energy needed to break old bonds is greater than the energy released in forming new bonds
No bonds are broken during the reaction
The energy released in forming new bonds is greater than the energy needed to break old bonds
Bond breaking releases energy and bond forming absorbs it
x: Breaking bonds absorbs energy and forming bonds releases it. If more energy is released by bond formation than is used in breaking, the net change is exothermic.

q: Which process is endothermic?
x: Breaking the H–H bond needs energy, so it is endothermic. Bond formation, lattice formation and neutralisation all release energy.

q: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −572 kJ. How much heat is released when 1 g of hydrogen burns? (H = 1)
x: 572 kJ is released for 2 mol H₂, which is 4 g. For 1 g: 572/4 = 143 kJ. Using 2 g per mole of the equation would wrongly give 286 kJ.

q: Which statement about photosynthesis and respiration is correct?
o: Photosynthesis is endothermic and respiration is exothermic
Photosynthesis is exothermic and respiration is endothermic
Both photosynthesis and respiration are exothermic
Both photosynthesis and respiration are endothermic
x: Photosynthesis absorbs light energy to build glucose, so it is endothermic. Respiration breaks glucose down and releases energy, so it is exothermic.

q: For the reaction X → Y, ΔH = −50 kJ. What is ΔH for Y → X?
x: Reversing a reaction keeps the size of ΔH but changes its sign. So Y → X has ΔH = +50 kJ and is endothermic.

q: In thermodynamics, the 'system' is:
o: The part of the universe chosen for study
Everything outside the part chosen for study
The wall that separates two regions
The total energy of the universe
x: The system is the part of the universe under study. Everything else is the surroundings, and the dividing surface is the boundary.

q: The real or imaginary surface that separates a system from its surroundings is called the:
x: The boundary divides the system from the surroundings. It may be real, like the walls of a beaker, or imaginary.

q: Which of the following is NOT a state function?
x: Work depends on the path by which a change is carried out, so it is not a state function. Enthalpy, internal energy and pressure depend only on the state.

q: A state function is a property whose change:
o: Depends on the path taken between two states
Is always equal to zero for any process
Depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path
Depends only on the time the process takes
x: A state function, such as enthalpy, has a change that is fixed by the initial and final states alone. Heat and work depend on the path.

q: The enthalpy, H, of a system is defined as:
x: Enthalpy is the internal energy plus the product of pressure and volume: H = E + PV. ΔE = q + w is the first law, not the definition of H.

q: The enthalpy change of a reaction is equal to the heat absorbed or released at constant:
x: ΔH = qp, the heat exchanged at constant pressure. Heat at constant volume equals ΔE, not ΔH.

q: The heat needed to raise the temperature of one mole of a substance by 1 K is called its:
x: Molar heat capacity refers to one mole. Specific heat capacity refers to 1 g (or 1 kg) of the substance.

q: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 50 g of water by 10 K? (specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)
The internal energy of a system is:
o: Only the kinetic energy of its molecules
Only the energy stored in its chemical bonds
The sum of all the kinetic and potential energies of its particles
The heat it can give out at constant pressure
x: Internal energy E is the total of all kinetic and potential energies of the particles. Its absolute value cannot be measured, only changes in it.

q: A gas expands by 0.010 m³ against a constant external pressure of 100 kPa. How much work is done by the gas?
x: Work = PΔV = 100 000 Pa × 0.010 m³ = 1000 J = 1 kJ. Using 100 Pa instead of 100 000 Pa gives a wrong small answer.

q: Hot tea is sealed inside a perfectly insulated flask, so neither heat nor matter can pass in or out. The tea is an example of:
x: An isolated system exchanges neither energy nor matter. A closed system exchanges energy but not matter; an open system exchanges both.

q: The SI unit of internal energy is the:
x: Internal energy, like all forms of energy, is measured in joules (J). The watt is a unit of power, the newton of force and the pascal of pressure.

q: One joule is equal to:
x: 1 J = 1 N m, and 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻², so 1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻². 1 kg m s⁻² is the newton.

q: A reaction releases 4500 J of heat. In kilojoules this is:
One calorie is equal to:
x: 1 cal = 4.184 J. The value 0.239 is the inverse relation (1 J ≈ 0.239 cal), and 4184 J is one kilocalorie.

q: One joule is the work done when:
o: A force of 1 N acts on a body for 1 s
A pressure of 1 Pa acts on an area of 1 m²
A power of 1 W is used over a distance of 1 m
A force of 1 N moves its point of application through 1 m in the direction of the force
x: Work = force × distance, so 1 J = 1 N × 1 m. Force acting for a time gives impulse, and pressure on an area gives force.

q: Enthalpy changes of reactions are normally quoted per mole, in the unit:
x: ΔH is energy per mole of reaction as written, so its unit is kJ mol⁻¹. kJ K⁻¹ is a heat capacity unit and J s⁻¹ is power.

q: Which product of units is equal to one joule?
x: 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻², so 1 Pa × 1 m³ = 1 N m = 1 J. This is why pressure × volume change (PΔV) is an energy term.

q: Which of the following is NOT a unit of energy?
x: The pascal (N m⁻²) is a unit of pressure. Joule, calorie and newton metre are all units of energy.

q: The first law of thermodynamics states that:
o: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, but can change from one form to another
Energy of a system always decreases in a spontaneous change
Heat always flows from a cold body to a hot body
The enthalpy change of a reaction depends on its path
x: The first law is the law of conservation of energy. The total energy of a system and its surroundings stays constant.

q: The first law is written ΔE = q + w. In this form, w stands for:
x: In ΔE = q + w, q is heat absorbed by the system and w is work done on the system. Work done by the system is then counted as negative.

q: A system absorbs 200 J of heat and does 50 J of work on the surroundings. What is ΔE of the system? (ΔE = q + w, w = work done on the system)
x: q = +200 J; work done by the system makes w = −50 J. ΔE = 200 + (−50) = +150 J. Adding 50 instead gives the wrong +250 J.

q: A system gives out 100 J of heat while 40 J of work is done on it. What is ΔE of the system? (ΔE = q + w, w = work done on the system)
x: q = −100 J (heat lost) and w = +40 J (work done on it). ΔE = −100 + 40 = −60 J.

q: A reaction is carried out in a sealed, rigid container so that its volume cannot change. Which statement is correct?
o: ΔE is always zero because the volume is fixed
No pressure–volume work is done, so ΔE equals the heat exchanged
The heat exchanged equals ΔH, not ΔE
Work done equals the heat absorbed
x: At constant volume ΔV = 0, so w = 0 and ΔE = q (written qv). The heat at constant pressure, not constant volume, equals ΔH.

q: Taking ΔE = q + w, which pair of events BOTH increase the internal energy of a system?
o: The system gives out heat and does work on the surroundings
The system absorbs heat and work is done on the system
The system gives out heat and work is done on the system
The system absorbs heat and does work on the surroundings
x: Heat absorbed makes q positive and work done on the system makes w positive. Only when both are positive must ΔE increase.

q: For an isolated system, the change in internal energy is:
o: Equal to the work done by the system
x: An isolated system exchanges no heat and no work with its surroundings, so q = 0, w = 0 and ΔE = 0.

q: A gas in an insulated cylinder (no heat exchange) is compressed by doing 300 J of work on it. Which statement is correct? (ΔE = q + w)
o: ΔE = −300 J and the temperature of the gas falls
ΔE = 0 because no heat is exchanged
ΔE = +300 J and the temperature of the gas rises
ΔE = +300 J and the temperature of the gas falls
x: q = 0 and w = +300 J, so ΔE = +300 J. The increased internal energy shows up as a rise in temperature.

q: For which reaction are ΔH and ΔE practically equal?
x: ΔH = ΔE + PΔV, and PΔV is significant only when the number of moles of gas changes. In H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl there are 2 mol of gas on each side, so ΔV ≈ 0.

q: The heat measured in a bomb calorimeter, where the reaction takes place at constant volume, gives directly the:
x: A bomb calorimeter is a sealed steel vessel, so volume is constant and q = ΔE. A ΔH value needs a constant-pressure measurement or a correction.

q: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and at the same time does 500 J of work on its surroundings. What is ΔE of the gas? (ΔE = q + w)
x: q = +500 J and w = −500 J (work done by the gas). ΔE = 500 − 500 = 0, so all the heat absorbed was used as work.

q: Hess's law states that:
o: The enthalpy change of a reaction depends on the number of steps
The total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whatever route is taken from reactants to products
The rate of a reaction is the same whatever route it takes
Heat absorbed by a system always equals the work it does
x: Hess's law of constant heat summation: ΔH depends only on the initial and final states, so all routes between them give the same total ΔH.

q: Hess's law is possible because:
o: Heat and work are state functions
Every reaction occurs in a single step
The rate of reaction depends on the path
x: Since enthalpy depends only on the state of the system, its change between two states cannot depend on the path. Heat and work are not state functions.

q: Given: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −394 kJ and CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −283 kJ. What is ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g)?
x: Route C → CO₂ equals C → CO plus CO → CO₂. So ΔH = −394 − (−283) = −111 kJ. Adding the two values instead gives −677 kJ.

q: A reaction X → Z goes through three steps: X → Y, ΔH = +30 kJ; Y → W, ΔH = −80 kJ; W → Z, ΔH = −10 kJ. What is ΔH for X → Z?
x: By Hess's law the steps add up: +30 − 80 − 10 = −60 kJ. Treating +30 as −30 gives −120 kJ.

q: ΔH of combustion of CH₄ = −890 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔHf of CO₂(g) = −394 and of H₂O(l) = −286 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔHf of CH₄(g)?
x: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O: −890 = [−394 + 2(−286)] − ΔHf(CH₄) = −966 − ΔHf, so ΔHf = −76 kJ mol⁻¹. Forgetting the 2 for water gives +210.

q: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −196 kJ. What is ΔH for SO₃(g) → SO₂(g) + ½O₂(g)?
x: Reversing the reaction changes the sign to +196 kJ, and halving it gives +98 kJ.

q: The lattice energy of NaCl cannot be measured directly. It is found from a Born–Haber cycle, which is an application of:
x: A Born–Haber cycle links the steps of forming NaCl from its elements; since the total ΔH is path-independent (Hess's law), the unknown lattice energy can be worked out.

q: Given: S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g), ΔH = −297 kJ and 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −198 kJ. What is ΔHf of SO₃(g)?
x: For 1 mol SO₃: S → SO₂ (−297) plus SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃ (−198/2 = −99). Total = −396 kJ mol⁻¹. Not halving gives −495.

q: A reaction X → Z has ΔH = −200 kJ. By another route, X → Y has ΔH = +50 kJ. What must ΔH be for Y → Z?
x: By Hess's law, ΔH(X→Y) + ΔH(Y→Z) = −200 kJ, so ΔH(Y→Z) = −200 − 50 = −250 kJ.

q: C(graphite) + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5 kJ; C(diamond) + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −395.4 kJ. What is ΔH for C(graphite) → C(diamond)?
x: Graphite → CO₂ → diamond: −393.5 + 395.4 = +1.9 kJ. Diamond has slightly more enthalpy than graphite.

q: H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −286 kJ and H₂O(l) → H₂O(g), ΔH = +44 kJ. What is ΔH for H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(g)?
x: Add the two steps: −286 + 44 = −242 kJ. Less heat is released when steam forms because some energy stays in the gas.

q: ΔHf values (kJ mol⁻¹): CaO(s) −635, CO₂(g) −394, CaCO₃(s) −1207. What is ΔH for CaO(s) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s)?
x: ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = −1207 − (−635 − 394) = −1207 + 1029 = −178 kJ.

q: The standard enthalpy of formation of a compound is the enthalpy change when:
o: One mole of the compound is formed from its elements in their standard states
One mole of the compound is burnt completely in oxygen
One mole of the compound is broken into gaseous atoms
One gram of the compound is formed from its elements
x: ΔHf° refers to one mole of compound made from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions. Burning is combustion; forming atoms is atomisation.

q: Which of the following has a standard enthalpy of formation equal to zero?
x: ΔHf° of an element in its standard state is zero. O₂(g) is the standard state of oxygen; ozone and diamond are not standard states, and water is a compound.

q: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy of formation of water?
x: Formation needs one mole of product from elements in their standard states (H₂ and O₂ gases). The second equation makes 2 mol, the third starts from atoms, and the last is neutralisation.

q: The standard enthalpy of combustion of a substance is the enthalpy change when:
o: One mole of oxygen reacts with the substance
One mole of the substance burns completely in excess oxygen under standard conditions
One gram of the substance burns in a limited supply of oxygen
One mole of the substance is formed from its elements
x: Combustion enthalpy is for complete burning of one mole of the substance in excess oxygen. It is always negative because combustion releases heat.

q: The enthalpy of neutralisation of any strong acid by any strong base is nearly the same, about −57 kJ mol⁻¹, because:
o: Every strong acid has the same molar mass
The salts formed all have the same lattice energy
Strong acids and bases are only partly ionised
The reaction in every case is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)
x: Strong acids and bases are fully ionised, so the only change is H⁺ + OH⁻ forming water. The other ions are spectators.

q: Compared with HCl, the neutralisation of ethanoic acid (acetic acid) by NaOH is:
o: More exothermic, because the weak acid releases extra energy as it ionises
Less exothermic, because some energy is used to ionise the weak acid
Exactly as exothermic, because the same amount of water forms
Endothermic, because weak acids absorb heat on reacting
x: Ethanoic acid is only partly ionised; some of the energy released is used to complete its ionisation, so less heat appears than about −57 kJ mol⁻¹. It is still exothermic.

q: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy of atomisation of chlorine?
x: Atomisation enthalpy is for forming one mole of gaseous atoms from the element in its standard state. Cl₂ → 2Cl makes two moles of atoms (that is the bond energy).

q: The enthalpy of atomisation of any element is always:
o: Negative, because atoms are more stable than molecules
Zero, because the element is in its standard state
Equal to the enthalpy of combustion of the element
Positive, because bonds or attractions between atoms must be broken
x: Separating an element into free gaseous atoms needs energy to overcome bonds or attractive forces, so atomisation is always endothermic.

q: 100 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl is mixed with 100 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Taking ΔH of neutralisation as −57 kJ mol⁻¹, about how much heat is released?
x: Moles of H⁺ = 0.1 dm³ × 1.0 = 0.1 mol, giving 0.1 mol of water. Heat = 0.1 × 57 = 5.7 kJ. Adding the moles of acid and base gives the wrong 11.4 kJ.

q: Burning 0.1 mol of a fuel raises the temperature of 500 g of water by 10 K. What is ΔH of combustion of the fuel? (c of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; ignore heat losses)
x: q = 500 × 4.2 × 10 = 21 000 J = 21 kJ for 0.1 mol, so 210 kJ per mole. Heat is released, so ΔH = −210 kJ mol⁻¹.

q: Standard enthalpy changes are quoted at a temperature of:
x: Standard thermochemical data refer to 25 °C, which is 298 K. 273 K is used for STP in gas calculations, not for standard enthalpies.

q: Which two enthalpy changes refer to the same chemical equation?
o: Combustion of methane and formation of methane
Formation of water and neutralisation of HCl by NaOH
Atomisation of hydrogen and combustion of hydrogen
Combustion of carbon (graphite) and formation of carbon dioxide
x: C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g) is both the combustion of one mole of carbon and the formation of one mole of CO₂ from its elements. The other pairs are different reactions.
